speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monteith (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF WELFARE GRANTS FOR RESEARCH, ETC.-ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL WELFARE COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an announcement to make which I believe represents a new breakthrough in Canada's welfare system.
26207-1-184
I have today written provincial ministers informing them of the government's intention to initiate a new program of welfare grants designed to assist in overcoming major deficiencies in our present nation-wide network of welfare services. By 1967 these grants will result in the channelling of $2,500,000 annually in federal funds into the fields of general welfare, professional training, and research. Nothing like this has ever been done in Canada before, and I hope there will be discussions with provincial authorities in the near future with a view to obtaining their full co-operation in an endeavour which I believe will strengthen tremendously Canada's welfare efforts.
There are two separate grants involved. The one pertaining to general welfare and professional training will commence at a level of $450,000 for 1962-63 and increase at the rate of $450,000 annually for five years, reaching $2,250,000 by 1966-67. The other grant respecting welfare research will begin at a level of $50,000 in 1962-63 and increase at the rate of $50,000 annually for five years, reaching an amount of $250,000 in 1966-67. Funds for the current fiscal year will be provided through a supplementary estimate.
This new program will be complemented by the establishment of a national council of welfare, as announced in the speech from the throne. I hope to make a statement very shortly indicating the membership of the council, one of whose first tasks will be to assist in working out the details of the new grants system. As I have indicated previously, I would also like the council to consider a number of other important social security matters such as the development of a new and integrated approach to public assistance, and the need for an increase in the level of benefits under family allowances along with the question of raising the age limit at which such allowances are paid in the case of children who are still attending school.
In taking these historic initiatives in relation to welfare, the government is anxious to furnish a balance to the emphasis which has long been placed on the provision of cash benefits. Income maintenance payments such as old age assistance, blindness and disability allowances, and unemployment assistance are vitally important, but in many instances their effectiveness has been reduced to some extent by the shortage of human resources

Health and Welfare
necessary to implement them fully. The welfare grants and the new council will, we believe, go a long way toward giving a more positive impact to these measures.
As far as the welfare research grant is concerned, we have seen the benefits which have accrued from scientific research in many fields, including health. We feel that similar gains may well be registered as a result of concentrated and organized study of human problems such as long term dependency and juvenile delinquency. A good deal of work is, of course, already being done in such areas and it is our hope that federal assistance will provide the necessary added impetus to these efforts.
The welfare research grant will be made available on a non-matching basis, while the general welfare and professional training grant will be on a matching basis with the provinces except for two of its aspects, scholarships and fellowships, including travel costs, and teaching and field instruction grants. Neither grant will be allocated among the provinces but both will be held in a central pool similar to the method followed for public health research under the national health grants program.
Projects relating to the field of corrections of concern to the Department of Justice will also be covered by this program through cooperation between our two departments.
Mr. Speaker, the government has received many representations calling for the kind of program we are now initiating. As the Prime Minister told the annual meeting of the Canadian Welfare Council in May, 1961, we have also had a frank exchange of views with representatives of welfare organizations about what should be done. As a result, the government is particularly aware of the many serious problems being encountered in the welfare field and has come to the conclusion that a national system of welfare grants affords the best approach to their solution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the first time in a decade all grain delivery points in western Canada have been placed on open quota. This marks the end of the longest period of elevator congestion in the history of Canada's grain trade. For ten years in succession restrictions on deliveries have had to be applied, so that grain producers who started farming since 1952 have never known a time of unrestricted deliveries.
The 1961 grain crop was a short one but of high quality and relatively few grades. This took the pressure off storage requirements. Coupled with this was the increased world demand for Canadian wheat that emptied elevator bins at an almost unprecedented rate.

Mr. Speaker, the end came today, when all delivery points were put on open quota by the wheat board.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ROLPHTON, ONT.  OPERATION OF NEW PLANT
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Veterans Affairs through whose department Atomic Energy of Canada is handled. Has the nuclear power plant at Rolphton gone into operation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minisier of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: ROLPHTON, ONT.  OPERATION OF NEW PLANT
speechtext:
The nuclear power plant at Rolphton, Ontario, became critical as the scientific term expresses it, at 2.40 a.m. yesterday, and considerable attention has been paid to this important event by the press of the country. The power station will not be fully effective, that is it will not be generating steam and transferring electricity into the Ontario grid until sometime later this year because of tests which must now be carried on to make sure that the reactor is working properly, but it is an important advance in the development of power from atomic sources.
The N.D.P. station has cost $33 million. It is a co-operative project among Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, Ontario hydro and the Canadian General Electric Company. It will have an electricity output of 20,000 kilowatts, and is the prototype for larger plants such as the 200,000 kilowatt Douglas point nuclear power station which is now under construction near the shore of lake Huron.

subtopic: ROLPHTON, ONT.  OPERATION OF NEW PLANT

subtopic: ROLPHTON, ONT.  OPERATION OF NEW PLANT

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED NON-PAYMENT OF SUPPLEMENTARY ALLOWANCES
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Has the minister seen a copy of a form letter sent out by the social allowances commission in Quebec to old age pensioners who were receiving supplementary allowances? If so, can he explain why the recipients have only now been informed that they are being paid for the last few months of last year and that they were no longer eligible for the supplementary allowances as from February 1, 1962?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monleilh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REPORTED NON-PAYMENT OF SUPPLEMENTARY ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
This situation seems to have been caused by the fact that the Quebec social allowances commission did not process until quite recently some applications they had received from pensioners for special assistance of this type. Welfare matters such as this are administered by the provinces, though my department pays one half the cost under the Unemployment Assistance Act. Under this act the provinces are free to grant whatever aid is required on the basis of individual need.
The Quebec commission seems to consider that on this basis some people at least do not require more than $65 per month. Thus the pensioners whose income was raised to that level by supplementary allowances are now receiving only federal old age security, which means that my department is paying all the extra cost instead of one half of it. Of course if the commission feels that in individual cases a higher payment is warranted, we would still be prepared to share the added cost under unemployment assistance.

subtopic: REPORTED NON-PAYMENT OF SUPPLEMENTARY ALLOWANCES
speechtext: I wonder if the minister could tell us what has been the reaction from British Columbia in regard to this cost sharing program.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REPORTED NON-PAYMENT OF SUPPLEMENTARY ALLOWANCES
speechtext: We have had no word whatsoever from the province of British Columbia, it being the only province from which we have not heard. We have no indication whether or not they intend to participate in the welfare increases.

Then we embarked upon the fourth set of supplementary estimates, commencing with the Department of Agriculture, about five minutes before five o'clock. On Monday, March 26, instead of continuing the supplementaries, as the government should have done and as the opposition asked, they were not called again until Wednesday, March 28. If they had been called at the beginning of that week they could easily have been concluded by March 30 and probably by March 29, particularly as items in nine various departments were passed on March 30.
Having failed to do that, the government should have called the supplementaries on April 2, and they could have been concluded at the latest by April 3. Instead they were held off until Friday, April 6, about one hour before five o'clock, by which time General McNaughton's interview was in the press. In other words the committee was given no consecutive opportunity to dispose of this business.
If one looks at the order of business one will find 10 items were given last night by the house leader as the business for today, the first item having to do with the electoral boundaries commission, and the next having to do with a measure concerning the Senate. speechtext: I should like to refer briefly to the matter of assistance to Eskimos in Labrador. In conjunction with the discussion that took place on the previous bill, No. S-9, which indicated a great deal of similarity, we believe this bill should also contain a provision that all directors of this company should at all times be Canadian citizens, ordinarily resident in Canada. This seems to be the stated policy of the Prime Minister and it appears to be in the interests of Canada. The sponsor has stated that the executive officers of this company are Canadians, ordinarily resident in Canada, and I wonder has he authority from the company to accept an amendment that all the directors of the company should at all times be Canadian citizens ordinarily resident in Canada.

Since discussion occurred last Tuesday on the previous bill I have secured some information for the committee which I think will probably satisfy the hon. members who raised this matter on the previous bill and who are now raising it on this one.
I am not prepared to accept an amendment which would require that all the directors of the company be Canadians, as the hon. member has suggested. I would point out that section 13 of the Small Loans Act states that all of the provisions of the Loan Companies Act shall apply in a case such as this. This company is being incorporated under the Small Loans Act and therefore all the provisions of that act will apply to this company. Section 19 of the Loan Companies Act reads as follows:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

I thank the minister, but I think there are some other points arising out of this upon which the minister could enlighten us. The minister will remember that during the discussion of the matter concerning the dispute some two years ago between railway operators and the non-operative groups the Prime Minister indicated the procedure to be adopted in so far as freight rates were concerned just as soon as the report of the royal commission was handed down.
Volume No. 1 of the royal commission's report was given to the house last session and volume No. 2 was tabled just about the time the house met in January of this year, but we still have no indication of what the government intends to do. I and others from this side have inquired of the ministry what the government intends to do with reference to these matters, and there has been no indication, other than the time honoured formula that when the policy of the government has been determined it will be announced in due course. Of course that can go on for months and years-
Twenty two years.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I hear one enlightened voice say 22 years and in reply I say that when the Turgeon royal commission brought down its recommendations we acted at once. We did not wait two years. We brought in all the recommendations by way of legislation and implemented them by way of legislation in the house, save one or two. However I do not want to get away from my question. Could the minister give some indication what the intentions of the government are, having regard to the statement of the Prime Minister and the recommendations of the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is, of course, a subject of very great importance. As the hon. member has said, volume 1 of the report of the royal commission came down in 1961 and volume 2 earlier this present year. Volume 1 contains far reaching recommendations affecting the operation of branch lines, unremunerative lines and passenger services, as well as several other features of the burdens borne by the railways.
That volume examined the fundamental position of the railways and the change which has come over the nature of railway operations in recent years. It took account of the fact that our railway legislation and our system of regulation carried out through the board of transport commissioners was adapted to a period when the railways enjoyed a virtual monopoly in the field of transportation, but that that situation has very greatly changed. In gist, this was the purport of volume 1.

In volume 2 the royal commission examines the fundamental question as to the basis of railway rate making, and again speaking very briefly, the commission has recommended some fundamental and far reaching changes in the whole basis of railway rate making. It is not going too far to say that the recommendations of the royal commission in this respect contemplate a radical departure from the basis of rate making as provided for in the present provisions of the Railway Act. As the hon. member is well aware, those provisions in the Railway Act have been unchanged in their substance for many years.
The two combined volumes of the report offer and would involve a fundamental reconstruction of much of our railway legislation, particularly on the financial and regulatory side, and these recommendations cannot be slurred over quickly. Because of their far reaching nature they require the most intensive study and they are receiving that study.
There have already been meetings with the presidents of the two transcontinental railways in regard to this subject. It is being actively pursued but I think I would be less than fair to the hon. member's inquiry and to the subject if I did not lay stress on the fact that this is one of the most important, far reaching recommendations that has come before a government from a royal commission for many a day and it will require, both on the part of government and in due course on the part of parliament, the most intensive study possible. I know the hon. member will not expect legislation based on the report to be coming before parliament at an early date.
In the meantime the government has asked parliament to make the necessary provision for the period during which the study is proceeding. We have on the order paper now a resolution in the name of the Minister of Transport contemplating an amendment of the Freight Rates Reduction Act to extend, but not beyond April 30, 1963, the period during which the revised rates under that act shall be applicable, and to increase the authorized expenditure under the act by an additional $15 million.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, parliament will be asked to appropriate a subsidy in the same sum as in 1961, namely $50 million, on terms similar to those attaching to the $50 million appropriation in 1961. This will meet the requirements of the railways, at least in part. In the meantime the action that parliament may see fit to take in due course on the report can take account of the necessity, if any, of dating the revisions made on behalf of the railways to suit the needs of the situation, taking into account
Supply-Privy Council at the same time these two provisions that parliament is being asked to make for this intervening period.

Mr. Chevriers I think I can take it for granted that the $50 million payment the Minister of Finance has in mind will not be brought down at this session of parliament. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I should like to put on record in Hansard exactly what the Prime Minister did say. Apparently the minister has taken objection to what I said earlier. I made the statement, and I stand by it, that we were never told at any time there would be two bites at the cherry. At no time was there any indication that we would proceed by stages in this matter. We were told that the recommendations would be brought down and that the house would act on them. Here is what the Prime Minister said as reported at page 359 of Hansard, November 30, 1960 dealing with the dispute which had arisen between the railways and the men. He said this, and I quote:
The reason we say we are waiting tor the report of the royal commission is this. It will make its report as to the means whereby these discriminatory rates may be avoided. Legislation will then be introduced in order to equalize opportunity across Canada. The companies may then make an application to the board of transport commissioners to raise the freight rates and to take into consideration the agreements now in existence between the employers and the unions back to January 1, 1960.
I asked the Prime Minister if he realized that this was bound to take some time; I had had some experience of these matters with the Turgeon commission. If hon. members will look at Hansard they will find the Prime Minister said the recommendations would be acted upon promptly. As the minister has said, the recommendations contained in volume 1 are of entirely different nature to those contained in volume 2. So it is difficult to understand why that statement or promise which was made by the Prime Minister was not implemented. After all, it was made almost two years ago. The Prime Minister surely knew the situation. He must have been in discussion with the members of the royal commission.
In so far as volume 3 is concerned, the minister knows better than I do that there will be no recommendations contained in that volume. At least, we have been told that that is the case. I believe the royal commission itself has made that clear in a press release. The third volume deals with technical matters, as the minister said, and is there to support either the first volume, or the second, or both volumes. So it is difficult to understand why it was not possible to implement the first part of the report.
A great deal was said by the Prime Minister about the effect of horizontal freight rates and how they were having a detrimental effect on the economy generally. I think there has always been general agreement on that. The only point which was at issue in that connection was how to do away with the unfavourable effect of the horizontal rates. The
Supply-Privy Council board of transport commissioners laid down several rulings in cases made public. The question is now whether volume 2 disagrees with what has been decided in those cases by the board of transport commissioners. I am not able to say, but I presume that the object of the first volume was to give these subsidies to the railways with that in mind. However, when I look at Hansard and at the statement made by the Prime Minister, which is to the effect that the moment the royal commission has made its report legislation will follow, the freeze will be lifted and the railways will be able to make their applications to the board of transport commissioners,
I am not so sure. In these circumstances I think the minister will understand at once that it is not an easy matter for those of us who sit on this side to understand what is the view of the government.
Coming to the $6 million which I mentioned earlier, the minister is right. I was in error. I was calling on my memory. In any event, it is $4,500,000 and it is still a substantial amount which will have to be found. True, it is over a period of three years. Then there is the additional amount which will be required if a settlement is brought about between the railways and the non-operative employees. These payments to which the minister has referred will not suffice. The $50 million he is going to bring down in a supplementary estimate, the portion of the $4,500,000 which he will be required to bring down for the C.N.R. in the same sort of estimate, will not cover the amount required in the event of a settlement of the dispute between the railways and the non-operative employees. The question arises: how are these capital sums to be found?

Is that a correct assumption?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think not, Mr. Chairman. Each of us can interpret the terms of the appropriation act of last session as he sees fit. The fact is that item 590 speaks of interim payments related to recommendations of the royal commission on railway problems pending its complete report.
Now, parliament did not say that it was approving those recommendations in their entirety. Parliament took note of those recommendations and with that knowledge apparently saw sufficient merit in them to regard it as desirable to make some specific provision for payment to the railways, and the method of allocation of that $50 million among the various railways was chosen simply in the light of the provisions of the Freight Rates Reduction Act. The railways and the method or terms of allocation are the same. That is the significance of the reference to the Freight Rates Reduction Act in item 590.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is one other point I wish to make. The minister has been endeavouring to answer my questions and I do not wish to pursue this matter unduly but there is another point I feel I should bring to the attention of the minister arising out of the payment of $50 million. I feel I should severely criticize the fact that payments are made to United States railways under this

legislation. Under the Freight Rates Reduction Act-that is, the one that is on the order paper and the previous one that was on the order paper last session-there are a number of United States railways which are receiving payments out of the $20 million for reducing their rates by 9 per cent as required by the order of the board of transport commissioners. It is understood that the $50 million subsidy we have been discussing is being divided among the carriers in the same manner as the $20 million subsidy. I ask my hon. friend to look at the royal commission report very carefully. There is nothing in the report of the MacPherson royal commission that recommends subsidies to the United States carriers. Their recommendations refer only to the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National Railways. The United States railways such as the New York Central in Ontario and Quebec, the Chesapeake and Ohio in Ontario, the Great Northern on the Pacific coast and the Midland Railway in Manitoba did not complain to the royal commission about losses on passenger service. So far as is known they do not have any unremunerative branch lines in Canada, except one of them, the Midland Railway of Manitoba, to a very small degree in the Crowsnest pass rates.
Bearing in mind that vote No. 590 we have been discussing refers to interim payments related to recommendations of the royal commission on railway problems pending its complete report, it is clear that none of the money covered by this vote should be paid to the United States carriers except perhaps a very small sum to the Midland Railway of Manitoba, as I have said, for participating in the Crowsnest pass rates.

This is the provision that parliament made in relation to item 590. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If I may be allowed just one word, I should just like to say this. My hon. friend seems to be under the mistaken apprehension that these moneys are going to United States railways operating in Canada. The royal commission on transportation made no recommendations giving the United States lines in Canada subsidies. That is the point that I am making. As to vote 590 to which the minister has referred, he stated that was in part to carry out and to implement the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will repeat my statement, I hope for the last time as I do not wish to see the committee detained unnecessarily. The $50 million was not provided to implement the report of the royal commission.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Then why refer to it at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will give the wording of item 590:
Interim payments, related to recommendations ... on railway problems-
In other words, parliament took into account that recommendation. But it also had before it the fact that there was a freeze on freight rates and there had been a withdrawal of the benefits that railways might have expected to receive under the last previous general increase in freight rates permitted by the board of transport commissioners. These were all taken into account. I think that is the answer to the hon. member's observation.
I just wanted to say that I was very pleased to hear the minister's statement that it was not the intention of the government to rush into any legislation arising out of the royal commission report.
They do not rush into anything.

I think it is obvious that volume 3 that we have coming from the royal commmission contains much of the supporting material on which their conclusions contained in volumes 1 and 2 were arrived at. It would seem to me that for the government to bring forward legislation and face the transportation agencies in Canada with it before that material is available would put them in a very unfair position. I am quite surprised indeed that the hon. member for Laurier should be urging that the government take quick action in this regard. I feel quite certain that the various transportation agencies in Canada have not even begun to be able to assess all of the implications of the far reaching proposals that have been made in the royal commission report. I was certainly pleased to hear the


minister's assurance that it is not the intention of the government to place the transportation agencies in that unfair position by rushing into any hasty legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall vote 735 carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. There are a couple of questions that I should like to ask the minister. One of the things that puzzle me about the royal commission on transportation is this. I understood or interpreted from statements made in this house by the Prime Minister over several years, and under repeated questioning, that the royal commission on transportation would have nothing to say about the Crowsnest pass rates, which I myself thought was an oversight and should have fallen within their terms of reference. Yet this matter was specifically ruled out. Nevertheless, the other day, in answer to a question that I had on the order paper namely question 374 we discover as follows:
The commission made an independent assessment of the studies and submissions and alternative figures arrived at by experts retained by the commission. Certain conclusions and estimates of the commission are contained in volume 1 of Its report. The commission has also reported that special studies will be included in volume 3 which has not yet been received by the government. No other estimates of the cost of moving such grain have been provided to the government during the past two years.
There are two oddities about this to me. One is that we have on the way this information from the royal commission about the Crowsnest pass rates when the Prime Minister specifically ruled out the possibility of any alterations or changes in the Crowsnest pass rates. I understand his words went along the line of phrases such as "sacred covenant" and something that was part of the tradition or almost the birthright of the western farmer.
And rightly so.
The Magna Carta.
And rightly so.

Yes, the Magna Carta; and the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tis-dale says "rightly so". If this is the case, what was this study of the Crowsnest rates so important for? Probably the reason we are still waiting for this volume 3 is this. I understand all the experts of the commission have been dispersed, and the commissioners. We know Mr. Mann now has a job heading up the national harbours board. I understand Mr. Anderson, the secretary, is back out west. What is the point of this study of the Crowsnest pass rates, especially in view of the Prime Minister's commitment that this matter was not going to be touched. I understand we are now going to have from this study what is considered to be the exact

expert figure of the burden that the railways are carrying in terms of loss between the revenue they get from the grain traffic and the actual cost of carrying it. This is most interesting information, that this is in hand. But I should like to have some explanation as to why the commission, it seems to me almost in defiance of the line set out by the Prime Minister, should get involved in this particular case.

May I ask the
hon. gentleman a question.
Yes.

Is it not a fact that while the Prime Minister said in the house on one occasion that the Crowsnest pass rates would not be involved, the terms of reference to the commission were not consistent with the assurance given by the Prime Minister?

I quite agree with the hon. member for Essex East. However, there is a related factor coming in here. On the very first day on which the commission met there was a long discussion as to its terms of reference and the whole question was introduced as to whether it could go into labour matters. I am sure the minister probably knows that after some discussion and some submissions it was assumed, on the basis of statements of the Prime Minister to parliament to quite an extent, that the whole question of railway labour was not to be touched on by this commission. I was at the first couple of hearings and I think my memory is correct that this was one of the main reasons why the whole problem of railway labour, which in many people's minds has been central to the predicament of the railways, was not considered, because there had been indications in the house that, though the matter was not strictly within the terms of reference of the commission to rule one way or the other, this was not the intention of the government. Yet we have the situation where this royal commission has bumbled its way into the Crowsnest pass rates picture and has come up with what I am sure will be claimed to be a solid figure showing the difference between the come and the go.
There is one other aspect of the recommendations of the royal commission that I find very ironical, and I wonder whether the minister has seen the irony. I should like to have his comments upon it. Certain newspapers have also picked up this point. I refer to the fact that by the time one has finished reading volume 2 of the commission's report it is apparent that the idea is that the railways are going to be freed at last to get out and compete. Subsidies are going to be 26207-1-186J
Supply-Privy Council wiped out. They are going to do away with the bridge subsidy which is a very real measure of help to the area from which I come. That kind of thing is an anachronism to me. They are not going to fiddle with all these subsidies in this new era of transportation into which we are moving. I know this found wide appeal, particularly in the newspapers of Canada which tend to be great free enterprise organs.
But here is the irony. How is this revolution going to be achieved? It is going to be achieved by more subsidies. We are going to wipe out the bridge subsidy which is designed to remunerate both railways and shippers of goods from eastern Canada to western Canada. The wiping out of that subsidy is something that is certainly going to affect traffic that moves through our area but according to the commission it has got to go. This is the anachronism. How are we going to get this new era under way? We are going to start handing out subsidies. The hon. member for Laurier referred to the total, almost $100 million. That is the great free competition and free enterprise of this new era. As the minister is the one who, in the short range picture at least, has to come up with these new subsidies, I am wondering whether he is aware that there is a certain paradox in the recommendations of the commission.
I should like to have his views on this matter.
There is another thing I should like to point out to the minister that I find ironical. Aside from the submission of the British Columbia government, it is almost impossible for me at least to find in the hearings any evidence upon which these thinkers on the royal commission base this whole new era of free enterprise and competition that is to be opened up for the railways. I have very grave doubts whether the commissioners really listened to the people who came to the hearings. I am making the assumption here that several people on the commission and probably one or two of the professional help theorized that what was needed in the railway picture was the opening up of competition and the freeing of the railways so that they could get into the fight and hold their own against the truckers and all other forms of transportation, and consequently they did not really pay any attention to the briefs that were presented.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise a point of order. I do not claim to know too much about the rules but it does seem to me that we seem to be discussing is the report of the commission, which will be open to discussion at another time. It also seems that certain assumptions are being made that the commissioners did not

Supply-Privy Council listen to some of the briefs presented to them. I would suggest that we are getting rather far afield.

On the point of order, we may be getting far afield but I suggest to the hon. member for Greenwood that the discussion started a few minutes after eight o'clock and for 35 minutes thereafter it ranged quite widely. I think it will be acknowledged that the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Laurier went into topics very much like this one, so I do not feel I am out of place in making these remarks. Really what I am doing is repeating an appeal to the Minister of Finance. Does he not think there is something bizarre in this whole theme of opening things up to competition and wiping out all these subsidies including the cutting down of some of the maritime subsidies that exist at the present time? The idea is that we are going to get back to competition, and yet at the same time the commissioners turn around and they are going to give the railways new kinds of handouts such as passenger subsidies for a time, branch line abandonment subsidies and so on. To me this is completely inconsistent, almost as inconsistent as the supposedly accurate study of the Crowsnest pass rates.
The other point I want to come back to is the question of the bridge subsidy. I should like to make the point to the minister that if this subsidy disappears it will be quite obvious that the very strong representations made by groups from our area at the hearings at Port Arthur completely failed to impress the commission. One of the factors that is central to defending our position and maintaining the link between eastern Canada and western Canada is the bridge subsidy or a subsidy of that kind; but that is to go out of the window.
As one of our local authorities on transportation matters, Mr. Charnock of the Fort William chamber of commerce, pointed out, this dream of competition is wonderful where you have competition in terms of traffic and in terms of carriers but in an area such as ours this kind of competition is very tenuous. What we are afraid of is something that is actually taking place at the present time in that a great deal of the automobile production of eastern Canada that is being shipped to western Canada, particularly to British Columbia, is being driven across the border, loaded on American rail carriers and shipped through to British Columbia rather than being transported the Canadian way. Will this removal of the bridge subsidy be another sample of the kind of steps that make us even less able to compete? While most of us are pleased at


the present time to have the kind of competition that exists to a degree between the truckers and the railroaders from the point of view of giving shippers an alternative, in our part of the country we still think that kind of competition in a transcontinental way is a pretty shadowy and insubstantial thing at the present time and that to think of opening it up is fantastic.
Another point I should like to make to the minister about the royal commission on railway problems has to do with the assumption it makes throughout that trucking is a mode of transportation in which it is very easy to get started because it does not require very much capital. All I know is that the C.N.R. has gone through about $15 million in the last couple of years getting into it. We do not know how much the C.P.R. has spent but it is a considerable sum of money. So we have these two big railway organizations going deeply into trucking and being encouraged now to go into it even more deeply, and we are led to believe that this is going to lead to a more and more competitive situation. I fail to see how it possibly can. I fail to see how a small or medium size public carrier on the highways can really compete in the long haul with what must be a monopolistic tendency on the part of the railways as they move into this field. It seems to me an encouragement to the railways that they have certainly welcomed.
I know a great many of the employees have welcomed the idea that at last they are going to be able to get in and compete with truckers, but I wonder if this is the way to do it. Are the trucking lines associated with the railways going to be required to pay income tax? Are Husband, East-West, Kingsway and all these lines now associated with the C.N.R. going to pay income tax? If they are not, then it is quite obvious that they have a competitive advantage over trucking lines that are not associated with the C.N.R.
To me it seems that the royal commission has raised almost as many problems as it solved, and it is for that reason I disagree with the hon. member for Laurier in his plea for urgency in tackling its recommendations. I hope the government proceeds slowly in regard to them, slowly enough so that we can bring a very strong case against the removal of the bridge subsidy until we can see there is some kind of salvation for this in the so-called competitive milieu that is going to be opened up.
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, for being carried away into areas detached from the specific question with which I started. I shall just repeat-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I can save the hon. member the trouble. I do not intend to make any comment on the acceptability or validity of any recommendation the commission has made. Aside from the acceptability of recommendations, what about the fact that this commission is coming up in volume 3 with figures on the loss pattern in the grain rates? Does the minister not consider this a contradiction of the statements that were made by the Prime Minister over a period of several years? speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has stated government policy in clear and unmistakable terms, and that is that as long as this government is in office the grain growers of western Canada are going to retain the full benefit of the Crowsnest pass rates. That is fundamental in the policy of the government.
The railways asked for determinations as to what they regarded as the loss they were incurring in carrying grain under the Crowsnest pass rates and the royal commission, at least in a divided report in this respect, made certain findings and certain recommendations as to how the alleged loss should be borne. But the statement of the Prime Minister is clear and abiding, that no thought will be given at any time to depriving the grain growers of western Canada of their rights in respect of the Crowsnest pass rates.

I should like to give an assurance on behalf of the party which will form the next government of Canada-and that probably quite soon-that the Crowsnest pass rates will be retained, as they were restored by a Liberal government after the first world war when they were torpedoed by the Tories.

I appreciate that the minister finds it difficult to deal with particular recommendations of the royal commission at this time. I also assume he would find it difficult to deal with omissions in the royal commission report with regard to representations made by communities about unfair, discriminatory rates, as they saw them, in so far as their competitive position is concerned in relation to other areas.
The community from which I come was joined by farm and labour organizations
Supply-Privy Council in the county of Essex and all through southwestern Ontario with regard to the inequitable freight rate structure which prevails in this area, as compared with other sections in the province of Ontario, notably the area that originates in Toronto eastwards.
The average freight rates between Windsor and Toronto are 25 per cent higher than those paid in the area from Toronto as far as Montreal. This imposes a heavy burden, not only on secondary industry in my section of the province, but also in the farming community. It is possible to ship a bushel of corn from Chicago to Montreal more cheaply than it is to ship a bushel of grain from Windsor to Montreal.
Having in mind the conditions prevailing in southwestern Ontario at the present time, particularly in the city of Windsor with regard to secondary industry and the consequential problem of unemployment that flows therefrom, it would seem to me, as it does to the Windsor industrial commission, to the chamber of commerce, to the labour organizations and others who have made recommendations to the effect that if the government is anxious to do something about these areas that are suffering from heavy unemployment, consideration ought to be given to alleviation of the inequitable freight rate structure which prevails in respect of the communities I have mentioned as compared to other sections of the province of Ontario and elsewhere.
The minister may say he cannot deal with this sort of thing at this time but the executive arm undoubtedly has the power of providing for a removal of these inequities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
In the past the executive has acted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

The minister says no but I beg to differ. In the past the executive has taken action to remove these inequities. One example of that was given in the statement made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate with regard to the Crowsnest pass rates. The traditional attitude taken with regard to that arises out of executive action, confirmed by various royal commissions, and reflected in the statement of policy enunciated by the minister just now. I do not quarrel with that. As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said, the Liberal party, when in office, took a position with regard to that. What I am now saying is that if the complaint which has been registered by the area from which I come is valid -and I believe it is-it is within the power of the government of Canada, the executive

Supply-Privy Council arm of government, to take action to remove these inequities. The minister has that power. This parliament has the power-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Parliament has, but not the executive.

When I say the executive I mean the executive has power to make recommendations which, in the form of legislative enactment, can rectify a situation which is felt to be unfair. If the government wants to do something about this grievance, and I believe there is a crying need, it has that power. I am not saying that the minister should tell us tonight what it proposes to do, but in the unhappy event that the hon. gentleman and his colleagues should ever be in power in the future, and that we greatly doubt, all I am saying to them now is that this is a matter in which the city of Windsor and southwestern Ontario generally are vitally interested. The brief that was presented by the Windsor industrial commission was supported not only by the city of Windsor and other communities in the county of Essex, but by communities all the way to London. This is a matter about which there is keen, and I think understandable, interest. I raise it tonight so that the minister can be forewarned once again of the position taken by these communities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if we are going to go into the complaints about the existing freight rates structure from individual communities in Canada, then we are certainly not going to reach item 729 tonight.
That does not alter the fact that a legitimate grievance can be mentioned.

speechtext:

Mr. Chairman, would the minister permit me to make a correction. I did say Toronto; I meant to say a bushel of corn from Chicago to Montreal.

speechtext: What is the hon. member comparing it with now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, I do reserve the right to talk outside the house as well as inside. I was asked about the O'Leary report and I said then, as I am prepared to say now, that this was a large subject in itself and it was more appropriate that it should be dealt with separately from the budget. That is why the Prime Minister said what was indicated in the course of yesterday's review of matters to come before the house. The house will have a better opportunity of dealing with this important and far reaching subject in the way proposed by the government than if it were submerged with many other subjects in the course of a general budget discussion.
When the hon. member portrays with mock grief and sympathy the humiliation which he sees heaped upon the Minister of Finance, let me say at once that I reject his miserable crocodile tears. I want no sympathy from any shedder of crocodile tears. The government has proceeded in a way which is beyond the understanding of those who had their governmental experience in dictatorial days. The hon. member simply does not understand why a government should attempt to follow a course which would give parliament the most effective and fullest opportunity to discuss a subject which is of great national importance.

1 cannot allow the statement made by the minister and the aspersions cast by the minister to go without reply. However, the reply will be brief, if the minister can contain his impatience, and then the question can be put. The only thing I can find to agree with in what the minister said was his use of the word "submerge" with respect to his budget. He said the government did not want the O'Leary recommendations submerged with the budget. I suggest that that is exactly what the government has in mind-submerging this budget, drowning it without a trace, and they wish they could do it, having heard what the public has to say about it. Perhaps the Prime Minister knowing how badly the budget was going to be received, wanted to associate the recommendations having to do with the O'Leary report with some other minister rather than the Minister of Finance. At no time that I can recall since confederation-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Have you been here since confederation? Who do you think you are?
I suggest to the minister that he can make his reply when I have concluded and when I can hear what he has to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, my lord.
Instead of doing the muttering he is doing from his seat-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was standing up.

That is a direct quote from the minister. As I was saying when the minister began muttering, at no time that I can recall has any minister of finance since confederation been humiliated the day after the budget by having the Prime Minister announce that something had been overlooked, or not dealt with, and that some other minister rather than the Minister of Finance was going to introduce tax changes. It is a profound humiliation. I do not say it is an undeserved humiliation, but it is a humiliation which no self-respecting minister of finance would endure for an instant. But we know of the humiliations which the minister has endured in that quarter, and having endured so many others, this, perhaps, is one more cross that he has decided to bear until those many crosses are made on the ballots which will put the minister out of his misery.
Are you going to lose?

I say this is a shocking way to treat parliament. The minister talks about other governments being dictatorial. No government since confederation has ever

gone on 12 days after the end of the fiscal year without getting its supply voted for the previous year. And why?
Obstruction.

Notwithstanding the biggest majority in history the Prime Minister goes on the air weeping crocodile tears and saying that he cannot control the House of Commons-that he cannot carry on the government; that he is paralysed by a handful of people in the opposition. That is the kind of self-confessed incompetence with which we have to deal, boasted about on the radio and on the television. If the Prime Minister believes he is incapable of getting the business of the country done, the sooner he ceases to try the better it will be for Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall be brief in my comment on this latest hysterical outburst. The hon. member speaks with great authority on things which have happened or have not happened since confederation. This, I suggest, is just one more of his indulgences in an arrogant type of boasting, but I will follow him in this-that I am sure that since confederation this chamber has not heard a more crocodile speech than that one.
We have an opportunity, now, to judge the earnestness, the genuineness, the sincerity of those protestations that we hear from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and others among his colleagues as to their eagerness to get on and debate item No. 729. This was the important item, they said, and they could not get to it fast enough. But you see what has happened, Mr. Chairman? We have been debating tonight for one and a half hours and we have passed one item. And here is the hon. gentleman prolonging this discussion by inviting a vote when he knows perfectly well that what is at stake here is whether the expenses incurred in the appointment and inquiries of the royal commission should be paid. This is what he is now proposing, that these expenses should not be paid. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that no crocodile could propose anything more irresponsible.

I am suggesting to you, sir, that this royal commission was totally and completely unnecessary, that any government that had even the most elementary capacity for decision would not have required any royal commission to go into this matter-

You
would have done nothing; just like the Liberal party.

This government has done nothing and it will do nothing. If the rumours that still float around this town are correct, there will be nothing whatever done by this
Supply-Privy Council parliament about the recommendations of the royal commission except to put things on the order paper that will never be implemented unless this session is going on a lot longer than most of the backbenchers supporting the government want it to. As the hon. gentleman said, nothing will be done about this matter.
Irresponsible opposition.

There is no earthly reason why many thousands of dollars should have been spent on this royal commission. The problem is a simple, obvious problem. It was dealt with by the previous government in a definite manner. Speaking of crocodile tears, I have never seen a crocodile shedding tears-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I am very hesitant to speak at this time for fear the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will accuse me of being Ilya Ehrenburg or some other Russian figure.
He is a great authority on Russians, too.

With respect to the hon. member's amendment let me say we do not lightly introduce amendments, and since support of this amendment would indicate that the commission and its recommendations are completely in disfavour with our party, which is not the case, we will vote against it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

On an item such as this 1 dislike bringing up an issue that involves my riding, but the Provincial Paper Mill in Port Arthur is the mill that provides paper not only for Reader's Digest and Time but also for most Maclean-Hunter publications. The minister is probably aware that the unions in that plant supported by other related groups have made representations to the government with regard to the likelihood of a loss of a minimum of 75 or up to 120 days work in a very busy mill.
The dilemma is this, and I wish to present it to the minister for a bit more information. If the recommendations of the O'Leary commission are not carried out we have an indication from Maclean-Hunter and other Canadian publishers that they will be forced to fold Canadian magazines such as Maclean's and Chatelaine and therefore out would go that part of the production of Provincial Paper Mills. On the other hand Reader's Digest and Time say that if the government proceeds with the legislation they will have to withdraw to the United States and out will go that part.
In a small way we have a problem for Solomon here. No matter which way the thing moves there is the likelihood that this particular paper mill, which is the largest producer in Canada of coated papers, is going to get it in the neck. I am sure the minister will appreciate why I am so anxious to know, as the representative of the people of that area, what negotiations the government has carried on with the various people involved so as to obtain some idea how much truth there is in the threat of Reader's Digest and Time that they are going to go back to the United States. For this reason I shall be very interested in the legislation when it is introduced to see to what extent it will come to bear on these companies.
I know the minister really cannot give much more information than he has but I


wish to ask him whether negotiations or discussions have taken place recently-by that I mean within the last three or four weeks- with the representatives of Reader's Digest and Time as to their likely course of action should the government implement the recommendations of the O'Leary report.

subtopic: SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I will try not to be long. I should like to comment briefly on this vote. Recently members received the publication "Canada and the United Nations, 1960". It is published by the Queen's printer under the auspices of the Department of External Affairs. This is the kind of document which has the story of the development of the United Nations and particularly Canada's part therein within recent years. At the beginning of this booklet there is a picture in which I think all Canadians will take pride. It is that of the Prime Minister of Canada addressing the 15th regular session of the United Nations general assembly. There is also an attractive portrait of Canada's Secretary of State for External Affairs presiding over a plenary meeting of the general assembly as one of the vice presidents of the general assembly. We all recognize the fact that a government in power will be publishing this kind of material. We welcome this kind of publication as being a part of their responsibility and adding to our knowledge of what its various departments are doing. Now, by way of contrast, I wish to mention something that has been disturbing a number of people.

subtopic: SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Name them.

subtopic: SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I have been asked by an hon. member in his seat to name them. I shall mention one person by name who brought this matter to my attention very recently. It was Dr. C. P. Wright who is British, who holds a Ph.D. degree and who has scholarly background in juridical matters and British constitutional procedure. Some time ago I placed on the order paper question 359 relating to the printing and the distribution of the bill of rights or the so-called bill of rights, since, when we examine the document in question of which 20,000 copies have been distributed all over Canada, we find that it really is not the bill of rights at all but is only a part of the bill of rights.
It actually appears to be part I but it is not that alone. The art work is of the finest. It is a tribute to the abilities of the artists on the staff of the Queen's printer, particularly Yvonne Diceman. If we take the answers given by the Secretary of State the other day it would appear that the idea was that of Yvonne Diceman and the Queen's printer alone.
[Mr. Pickersgill.l

Here is a document which has gone all over the country in volume. It has gone to many schools and many areas where there are new Canadians and people with very limited knowledge of legal and constitutional matters and civil liberties. Here we have a part of the act with the most beautiful art work possible. The heraldic work is excellent. But with part I of the act there is also an extract from the speech of the Prime Minister, with the words underneath, "The Right Honourable John G. Diefenbaker, Prime Minister of Canada, House of Commons Debates, July 1, 1960". In ink of another colour is the signature of the Prime Minister and it would appear as though he had signed each individual copy.

subtopic: SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I thank the supporters of the government for their applause but I think there is a principle involved here and we have to have courage enough to stand up and say that under these circumstances this is not a proper expenditure of the public printing and stationery branch. I would ask hon. gentlemen in this house, and we are all gentlemen-

subtopic: SECRETARY OF STATE

subtopic: SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes, except the more beautiful and talented members of the house- to consider what they would think if, for example, when old age pensions were introduced or the veterans charter or legislation relating to NATO or family allowances or the St. Lawrence seaway, the Queen's printer and the heraldic artist had produced a document of this kind over the signature of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent or the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King. There would have been outcry from coast to coast.

speechtext: And properly so.

subtopic: SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Actually many lawyers were concerned about the bill of rights. I do not intend to touch on that aspect but I do intend to touch on the fact that this particular document with all this art work which has been distributed at public expense has been used deliberately to convey the false impression that this country has received new liberties and that these are the gift of the gentleman who now presides as Prime Minister of Canada.
